    In plain words

    N-able says hackers are taking advantage of a flaw in its N-central software that can let them get in without properly signing in and take over administrator accounts. This affects customers running N-central on their own servers unless they install the new hotfix, while hosted customers have already been updated. It matters because N-central is used by managed service providers and company IT teams to manage many computers and network devices, so a break-in could spread beyond N-able’s direct customers.

    Summary
    N-able says attackers are actively exploiting an authentication bypass flaw in N-central that can enable administrative account takeover. Hosted systems have been patched, but on-premises customers should urgently install hotfix 2026.3.1.7 and check for the provided indicators of compromise.

    N-able is warning customers that hackers are exploiting an authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577, affecting hosted and on-premises N-central servers. The company released hotfix 2026.3.1.7 to address the issue, which affects all N-central versions before 2026.3. Hosted deployments have already received the update, while on-premises customers need to install it manually.

    N-central is N-able’s Remote Monitoring and Management platform, used by managed service providers and corporate IT departments to manage large groups of systems and network devices. Because of this role, a compromise of N-central servers can allow attackers to extend activity beyond N-able’s direct customers. The product was also targeted last year in zero-day attacks that prompted CISA to issue an urgent alert.

    CVE-2026-18577 resulted from an incomplete patch for CVE-2026-18576, and both vulnerabilities could be exploited for administrative account takeover. N-able has not shared technical details or the number of customers targeted or compromised through CVE-2026-18577. The company provided indicators of compromise, including four IP addresses, a registered service named “Cloudflared,” and “svchost.exe” in users’ documents folders, and advised affected customers to contact N-able support and engage their security teams.

    • On-premises N-central customers carry the immediate remediation burden because hosted deployments have already been updated, but self-managed instances require manual installation of the hotfix.
    • The new flaw is especially concerning because it resulted from an incomplete fix for a prior authentication bypass issue, meaning customers who addressed the earlier vulnerability may still remain exposed without the latest hotfix.
    • N-able’s indicators of compromise highlight abuse of legitimate-looking components, including Cloudflared and a file named “svchost.exe” placed in users’ documents folders, so customers should not treat familiar names as automatically benign.
    • The risk extends beyond N-able’s direct customers because N-central is used by managed service providers and IT teams to manage large numbers of systems and network devices.
    Key Points
    • 01N-able warned that hackers are exploiting an authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577, affecting hosted and on-premises N-central servers.
    • 02N-able released hotfix 2026.3.1.7 to address the issue, which affects all N-central versions before 2026.3.
    • 03Hosted N-central deployments have already received the update, while on-premises customers must install it manually.

    • 05N-able provided indicators of compromise including four IP addresses, a registered service named “Cloudflared,” and “svchost.exe” in users’ documents folders.

In plain words

Attackers broke into N-able N-central servers, which are used by service providers and IT teams to manage many customer computers, after an earlier fix from N-able did not fully solve the problem. This means affected providers could have had attackers use one central management system to reach computers belonging to multiple customer organizations. N-able says everyone using N-central should update to version 2026.3.1.7, and affected customers also need to look for hidden remote access left behind on the managed computers because updating the server will not remove it.

Summary
Attackers exploited an authentication bypass in N-able N-central to take over servers and access managed customer endpoints, and N-able says its initial fix was incomplete. Customers must upgrade to 2026.3.1.7 and check endpoints for persistent Cloudflare tunnel services or other signs of compromise.

N-able said attackers exploited an authentication bypass in N-central to gain remote administrative access and reach customer systems managed through those servers. The company said its first fix was incomplete, and CVE-2026-18577 affects N-central builds prior to 2026.3.1.7. N-able shipped build 2026.3.1.7 on August 2 as the first unaffected version.

After compromising an N-central server, the attackers used Take Control to reach managed endpoints and registered Cloudflare tunnels as services on the devices. N-able said the tunnels preserved access after the route through the N-central server was revoked, and the disclosure does not suggest Cloudflare was compromised. Customers that find evidence of compromise must hunt for and remove malicious tunnel services from managed endpoints because upgrading N-central does not remove persistence installed on another machine.

N-able began investigating on July 31 after an unusual volume of licensing errors from on-premises customers and said it contacted a limited number of affected customers. Huntress said it observed exploitation involving one self-hosted N-central instance within one partner account, with attackers accessing nine organizations under that account and reaching one endpoint in each. N-able has not disclosed the number or identities of affected customers, how many downstream devices were reached, when exploitation began, who is behind it, or whether any data was taken.

  • Upgrading only to N-central 2026.3 is not sufficient because N-able’s first instruction was superseded by the 2026.3.1.7 hotfix as the first unaffected build.
  • Remediation cannot stop at patching N-central because the attackers allegedly placed Cloudflare tunnel services on managed endpoints that could keep access alive independently of the compromised server.
  • Matches against N-able’s published attacker IP addresses need careful correlation because Huntress identified several of the initially listed addresses as Mullvad or NordVPN exit nodes.
  • Logs showing Take Control activity are not automatically proof of compromise because Huntress said the same logs also appear during legitimate Take Control use.
  • N-able’s CVE records do not identify the vulnerable endpoint or request sequence, and the company has not published code-level root-cause details.
Key Points
  • 01N-able said attackers exploited an authentication bypass in N-central to gain remote administrative access and reach customer systems managed through those servers.
  • 02N-able said its initial fix was incomplete, and CVE-2026-18577 affects N-central builds prior to 2026.3.1.7, which was shipped on August 2 as the first unaffected version.
  • 03After compromising an N-central server, the attackers used Take Control to reach managed endpoints and registered Cloudflare tunnels as services on the devices to preserve access after the N-central route was revoked.
  • 04N-able told all N-central customers to upgrade to 2026.3.1.7 and said customers with evidence of compromise must also hunt for and remove malicious tunnel services from managed endpoints.
  • 05Huntress said it observed exploitation involving one self-hosted N-central instance in one partner account, with attackers accessing nine organizations under that account and reaching one endpoint in each.

Russian hackers hijack hotel Wi-Fi networks to spy on travelers, Microsoft says
therecord.media · 03 Aug 2026 12:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5

In plain words

Microsoft says Russian government-linked hackers have been breaking into hotel and hospitality Wi-Fi systems and steering guests to fake sign-in or update pages. Travelers, especially people on work trips, can have their account passwords stolen or be tricked into installing harmful software that lets the hackers spy on their computers. The activity has affected hotels and other shared venues in several countries, and similar places like airports, conference centers, universities, and co-working spaces could also be at risk.

Summary
Microsoft says Russian state-backed hackers tied to Midnight Blizzard are compromising hotel and hospitality Wi-Fi captive portals to steal travelers’ Microsoft 365 credentials and deliver espionage malware. The campaign targets corporate travelers globally and may affect other shared venues such as conference centers, airports, and co-working spaces.

Russian state-sponsored hackers have been compromising hotel Wi-Fi networks around the world to steal travelers’ login credentials and infect devices with espionage malware, according to Microsoft. The company linked the activity to Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard that Western intelligence agencies believe is connected to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. The campaign, first observed by Microsoft in early May, targets hotels and other hospitality venues that require guests to log into Wi-Fi through captive portals.

The attackers manipulate internet traffic on compromised networks to redirect victims to fake Microsoft login pages or fraudulent browser and operating system update screens. Microsoft said one technique allows attackers to intercept credentials and gain access to Microsoft 365 accounts, while another uses ClickFix social engineering to trick users into installing malware themselves. ReliaQuest, which first disclosed the activity in July, said hotels and other hospitality organizations in multiple U.S. cities, India, and Saudi Arabia have been affected, with corporate travelers appearing to be the primary targets.

Microsoft identified two malware families used in the campaign: CornFlake and ChocoShell. CornFlake is a remote access trojan that can maintain control of infected Windows computers, collect files, record keystrokes, steal passwords and tokens, capture audio and video, detect USB drives, and allow remote control. ChocoShell is designed to quickly harvest browser cookies, saved passwords, Microsoft 365 single sign-on tokens, and Wi-Fi credentials, and Microsoft said some fake update pages also direct Android users to install a malicious application.

  • The campaign turns trusted shared Wi-Fi login pages into a credential-theft and malware-delivery channel, meaning the risk begins before travelers fully connect to the internet.
  • The attackers use different paths depending on the victim interaction: fake Microsoft sign-in pages to capture Microsoft 365 credentials and fake update prompts to persuade users to install malware themselves.
  • Microsoft’s attribution to Storm-2945 differs from ReliaQuest’s earlier assessment pointing to APT28-like tactics, showing that similar router or traffic-hijacking methods can complicate attribution.
  • The use of ChocoShell to steal Microsoft 365 single sign-on tokens and browser cookies means attackers may be able to access cloud services without relying only on stolen passwords.
  • Microsoft noted that some fake update pages include instructions for Android users, indicating the operation may be moving beyond Windows computers.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft said Russian state-sponsored hackers linked to Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, have been compromising hotel Wi-Fi networks to steal travelers’ login credentials and infect devices with espionage malware.
  • 02The campaign targets hotels and other hospitality venues that use captive portals, redirecting victims to fake Microsoft login pages or fraudulent browser and operating system update screens.
  • 03ReliaQuest said the activity has affected hotels and other hospitality organizations across multiple U.S. cities, as well as in India and Saudi Arabia, with corporate travelers appearing to be the primary targets.
  • 04Microsoft identified two malware families used in the campaign: CornFlake, a remote access trojan for persistent control of Windows computers, and ChocoShell, an information stealer for harvesting credentials and tokens.
  • 05ReliaQuest warned that organizations operating captive portal networks, including airports, conference centers, co-working spaces, universities, healthcare facilities, and event venues, could become targets.

In plain words

A criminal group called INC Ransomware is increasingly taking advantage of recently fixed weaknesses in SonicWall SMA 1000 devices, which companies and governments use to let people connect to internal networks from outside. Victims listed by the group include private sector and government organizations in countries such as Australia, the U.S., the U.A.E., Colombia, and Switzerland. The concern is that attackers can use these weaknesses to steal login details and security-code settings, keep access for a long time, move deeper into an organization’s network, and pressure victims through emails and phone calls.

Summary
INC Ransomware has become the main group exploiting patched SonicWall SMA 1000 zero-day flaws to steal credentials, MFA seeds, and session data for persistent access and lateral movement. Organizations using SMA 1000 appliances should patch immediately and perform threat hunting, credential rotation, and integrity checks.

INC Ransomware has emerged as the “dominant threat actor” exploiting recently disclosed flaws in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access 1000 series VPN appliances. Resecurity reported that the group accelerated activity from the beginning of August 2026 and listed multiple victims on its data leak site. Ransomware.Live statistics cited in the article say the group has claimed 885 victims to date, with the most recent listed on August 2, 2026.

The attacks are suspected to involve chaining CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410 to enable arbitrary command execution and takeover of vulnerable devices. SonicWall released fixes for the two flaws in mid-July 2026, and the flaws are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days. Rapid7 said attackers used access to extract high-value credentials, active session databases, and Time-Based One-Time Password multi-factor authentication seed configurations to support persistent access and lateral movement.

Volexity attributed pre-disclosure exploitation starting June 22, 2026, to a threat cluster it tracks as UTA0533, involving KNUCKLEBALL, Suo5, and ORANGETAIL. Resecurity said INC Ransomware victims listed between July 17 and August 1, 2026, included private sector and government organizations from Australia, the U.S., the U.A.E., Colombia, Switzerland, and other countries. Customers are advised to patch SMA 1000 appliances, conduct threat hunting, rotate credentials, and verify integrity, including reviewing external sources that interacted with /wsproxy or used unusual parameters.

  • Patching alone may not be sufficient for already-exposed SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances because the article says attackers extracted credentials, active session databases, and TOTP MFA seed configurations that could support long-term access.
  • Threat hunting should specifically examine external source addresses that interacted with the /wsproxy path or used unusual parameters, then correlate those events with internal authentication and lateral-movement activity.
  • Victim organizations should treat unsolicited ransomware “help” calls or emails as part of the extortion pressure campaign, as Resecurity reported contacts from unknown organizations and an individual using the name “Andrew” and the email address info@helprans[.]com.
  • The overlap between Rapid7 and Volexity findings suggests defenders can connect activity involving KNUCKLEBALL, Suo5, ORANGETAIL, and the SonicWall SMA flaw chain when investigating possible compromises.
Key Points
  • 01Resecurity reported that INC Ransomware has emerged as the dominant threat actor exploiting recently disclosed flaws in SonicWall SMA 1000 series VPN appliances.
  • 02The attacks are suspected to chain CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410 to enable arbitrary command execution and takeover of susceptible devices, with fixes released by SonicWall in mid-July 2026.
  • 03Rapid7 said the zero-day attacks were used to extract high-value credentials, active session databases, and Time-Based One-Time Password multi-factor authentication seed configurations to support persistent access and lateral movement.
  • 04Volexity attributed pre-disclosure exploitation starting June 22, 2026, to a threat cluster it tracks as UTA0533, involving the Python script KNUCKLEBALL, the Suo5 HTTP proxy, and the ORANGETAIL Java web shell.
  • 05Resecurity said new victims listed by INC Ransomware between July 17 and August 1, 2026, included private sector and government organizations in Australia, the U.S., the U.A.E., Colombia, Switzerland, and other countries.

In plain words

Coinkite, the Canadian company behind the Coldcard bitcoin storage device, said thieves used a flaw in the device’s software to steal at least $88.6 million in bitcoin from thousands of customer addresses. The company destroyed remaining devices that still had the flawed software, stopped shipping them, and released a fixed version. This matters because people bought these devices to keep their bitcoin safer offline, yet some users still lost large amounts of money, and the company has not said whether victims will be compensated.

Summary
Coinkite destroyed remaining Coldcard hardware wallet inventory running vulnerable firmware after hackers exploited an old seed-generation flaw to steal at least 1,367 BTC, worth about $88.6 million, from thousands of addresses. The company has released patched firmware and is urging affected users not to discard devices as recovery and law enforcement efforts continue.

Coinkite, the Canadian company behind the Coldcard bitcoin hardware wallet, said it destroyed remaining inventory made with vulnerable firmware after customers reported bitcoin thefts. The devices are used to store bitcoin offline instead of on an exchange. The company confirmed that a vulnerability previously discovered in March 2021 is now being used to breach accounts.

Galaxy Research said the hackers behind the campaign stole at least 1,367.05 BTC, worth about \(88.6 million, from 4,585 addresses. Chainalysis said two of the biggest victims lost a combined \)4 million and that the attacker appeared to target high-value wallets early. According to Chainalysis, the cumulative value stolen reached roughly $30 million in the first 10 minutes.

Coldcard said it has been working with customers to move funds and told affected users not to dispose of their devices because they may become important if funds are recovered. The company released patched firmware that it says prevents the issue going forward, and said it halted shipments and destroyed affected inventory because devices could not be upgraded until users initialized them. The FBI declined to comment on whether it is investigating, and Coinkite did not respond to questions about whether it will compensate victims.

  • Coldcard told affected users not to dispose of their devices because the hardware may become important if stolen funds are recovered and legal teams coordinate with law enforcement.
  • The company said affected devices could not simply be upgraded before shipment because their high-security locks prevent firmware upgrades until a user initializes the device.
  • Chainalysis said the attacker appeared to study the victim wallet population before the theft, based on the early targeting of high-value wallets.
  • A Coinkite senior official blamed the incident partly on AI-assisted code reviews, saying they may help criminals find old bugs faster than experts can address them.
Key Points
  • 01Coinkite said it destroyed its remaining Coldcard inventory manufactured with vulnerable firmware after reports that customers were being robbed of bitcoin.
  • 02Galaxy Research said the hackers behind the campaign stole at least 1,367.05 BTC, worth about $88.6 million, from 4,585 addresses.
  • 03Coldcard released patched firmware that it says prevents the issue going forward and said it has been working with customers to move funds.
  • 04Chainalysis said the attacker prioritized high-value wallets, causing the cumulative stolen value to reach roughly $30 million in the first 10 minutes.
  • 05The FBI declined to comment on whether it is investigating the campaign, and Coinkite did not respond to questions about whether it will compensate victims.

Targeted Attack on Government Entities in the Middle East | Part 2

In plain words

Researchers analyzed a newly identified tool called BINDCLOAK that was used against government entities in the Middle East after attackers had already broken into victim machines. The tool lets the attackers secretly communicate with infected computers, load extra add-ons, gather information, and try to run parts of itself with higher privileges. This matters because the same group had previously been linked to attacks in Central Asia, and this campaign shows it expanding operations into the Middle East with a focus on the energy sector.

Summary
ThreatLabz analyzed BINDCLOAK, a newly documented modular Windows backdoor used in targeted attacks on Middle Eastern government entities and assessed with high confidence to be a variant of OctLurk. The malware uses encrypted TLS-based C2, reflective plugin loading, token abuse, and EDR-evasion techniques, showing a sophisticated East Asia-linked actor expanding operations beyond Central Asia.

ThreatLabz published a technical analysis of BINDCLOAK, a previously undocumented 64-bit modular Windows backdoor written in C++. The backdoor was deployed on victims’ machines during post-compromise activity in a multi-stage attack chain targeting government entities in the Middle East. BINDCLOAK was decrypted and reflectively loaded by the MIXEDKEY loader, which was covered in Part 1 of the research.

ThreatLabz assesses with high confidence that BINDCLOAK is a variant of OctLurk. The assessment is based on key code similarities between BINDCLOAK and OctLurk, as well as shared command-and-control infrastructure. The article also states that the campaign represents an expansion of victimology from Central Asia to the Middle East, with a key focus on the energy vertical.

BINDCLOAK uses a complex message routing mechanism to manage communication with its command-and-control server over TLS on TCP connections. It generates a host identifier from the computer name and C:\ volume serial number, sends a beacon containing host information, and encrypts messages using zlib compression and two layers of rolling XOR encoding. The backdoor supports commands for collecting user tokens, starting and stopping modules with user or process tokens, loading plugin DLLs reflectively, and calling SetThreadExecutionState to help prevent the infected machine from entering sleep mode.

  • BINDCLOAK’s C2 encryption sends the randomly generated second XOR key in cleartext, meaning the confidentiality of its traffic depends mainly on obscurity and the hardcoded first XOR key rather than keeping all encryption material secret.
  • The plugin loader deliberately routes LoadLibraryW calls through RtlQueueWorkItem to avoid suspicious API calls from unbacked executable memory regions, showing the malware was designed with specific EDR detection logic in mind.
  • The threat actor’s reuse of the same SSL certificate across cert.hypersnet[.]com and the OctLurk domain about.blsouqs[.]com provides a concrete infrastructure link between BINDCLOAK and previous OctLurk activity.
  • BINDCLOAK’s GET_STATUS command collects process ownership and token permission details, giving the operator a built-in way to choose processes or credentials for privilege elevation before starting modules.
  • The campaign’s observed move from Central Asia to Middle Eastern targets, with a focus on the energy vertical, marks an expansion in victimology attributed to the same actor behind OctLurk.
Key Points
  • 01BINDCLOAK is a previously undocumented 64-bit modular Windows backdoor written in C++ and deployed on victim machines during post-compromise activity.
  • 02BINDCLOAK was decrypted and reflectively loaded by the MIXEDKEY loader in a multi-stage attack chain targeting government entities in the Middle East.
  • 03ThreatLabz assesses with high confidence that BINDCLOAK is a variant of OctLurk based on code similarities and shared command-and-control infrastructure.
  • 04BINDCLOAK uses a complex message routing mechanism and encrypted TLS-over-TCP communication to manage its command-and-control channel.
  • 05The backdoor supports commands for collecting user tokens, starting and stopping modules with user or process tokens, reflectively loading plugin DLLs, and preventing the infected machine from entering sleep mode.

The article provides concrete technical details, infrastructure links to OctLurk, and actionable indicators and techniques relevant to defenders tracking targeted intrusions.

In plain words

An unknown Chinese-speaking group is using leaked attack software called DarkSword to target Apple iPhones through fake AWS and Apple ID sign-in pages. People using affected iOS versions could have sensitive information such as iCloud, Wi-Fi, keychain data, and files stolen after visiting one of these pages. This matters because a tool once linked to spying groups is now publicly leaked and being reused by more attackers across infrastructure in several countries.

Summary
A Chinese-speaking threat actor is using the leaked DarkSword iOS exploit kit through fake AWS and Apple ID pages to compromise iPhones and deploy the GHOSTBLADE data-stealing implant. The campaign includes multiple exposed admin panels and infrastructure across several countries, showing that the leaked kit is being actively reused beyond its original operators.

An unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor has been observed targeting Apple iOS devices by using a publicly leaked version of the DarkSword exploit kit. Censys identified the actor operating more than 100 web properties, most of them fake AWS sign-in pages on a domain that also hosts the exploit toolkit. The hosting is concentrated in Hong Kong but also extends into Japan, the United States, and Europe.

DarkSword is a full-chain exploit kit that targets iOS versions 18.4 through 18.7 and has been linked to campaigns affecting Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine since at least November 2025. The kit uses watering-hole pages to trigger now-patched Apple vulnerabilities, run JavaScript, and deploy the GHOSTBLADE information-stealing malware. Its use has expanded after the public leak of its source code, allowing additional threat actors to adopt it.

Censys found multiple related panels, including DarkSword Admin, Decode Dashboard, and C2 Control Panel, as well as hosts tied to fake AWS and Apple ID sign-in pages. The attack flow begins when a victim reaches an operator-controlled domain, which loads a malicious iframe that runs the DarkSword chain and deploys GHOSTBLADE modules. After successful exploitation, the implant dumps keychain, iCloud, and Wi-Fi credentials, exfiltrates files, and sends the collected data to attacker-controlled endpoints.

  • The campaign appears to use the publicly leaked DarkSword kit rather than a custom reimplementation, based on a shared staging-page hash and Russian-language code comments preserved from the leaked source.
  • The same infrastructure cluster blends credential-harvesting decoys, exploit delivery, malware control panels, and data-extraction dashboards, indicating the operator can manage multiple stages of the operation from related hosts.
  • A Singapore-based host linked to this activity also hosted a Coruna administration panel, showing that the operator’s infrastructure is not limited to DarkSword and overlaps with another iOS exploit kit.
  • The C2 Control Panel exposed unusually direct attribution clues, including the group name “Asia-Pacific Group” in Chinese and a visible Telegram contact link.
  • An open directory in Frankfurt exposed operational tooling, including an SSH key comment, a web-content fuzzer, and references to the previously undocumented Thorn C2 malware family.

A cyberattack on the U.K.’s Police National Legal Database compromised contact data of more than 100,000 police officers and other criminal justice professionals. The intrusion was detected on Sunday, July 26, and was later claimed by the ExfilSquad data extortion group. PNLD is an online legal resource service used by the 43 Home Office police forces in England and Wales, as well as the British Transport Police.

PNLD said the exposed data includes full names, organizations, and email addresses of police officers, staff, criminal justice professionals, and government partners. Names and email addresses of Ask the Police users who submitted a question through the platform are also considered compromised. PNLD said it has found no evidence that passwords or other security credentials were compromised, and that it does not hold confidential information relating to victims, witnesses, or offenders.

ExfilSquad claimed it stole 1.9 GB of data from PNLD, including approximately 135,000 records belonging to 114,000 PNLD subscribers and 21,000 Ask the Police users. The group published sample data to support its claims and demanded a ransom in exchange for not releasing the remaining stolen data. The incident is being investigated with assistance from cybersecurity experts and the National Crime Agency, and the Information Commissioner’s Office has been notified.

  • The breach affected both a police-facing legal resource and the public-facing Ask the Police service, showing that a single PNLD incident exposed contact details from internal professional users and members of the public who submitted questions.
  • Although PNLD says no passwords or confidential victim, witness, or offender data were affected, the exposed names, organizations, and email addresses still identify police and criminal justice personnel at large scale.
  • The affected PNLD user base is broad because the service is used by the 43 Home Office police forces in England and Wales as well as the British Transport Police.
  • ExfilSquad’s claim that it stole 135,000 records is higher than PNLD’s statement that more than 100,000 people were affected, indicating that the attacker’s claimed dataset includes both PNLD subscribers and Ask the Police users.

In plain words

Attackers are copying popular GitHub pages for AI tools and developer resources, then hiding harmful downloads inside them or changing installation links so people trust and run them. The main targets are AI users and software developers, especially in North America, Asia, and Southern Europe, with financial services, banking, and technology organizations most affected. This matters because developers often have access to source code, cloud logins, secret keys, and software release systems, so stealing from their computers could lead to wider attacks on other people and companies.

Summary
Attackers are cloning popular AI and developer GitHub repositories to trick users into running a multi-stage SmartLoader chain that delivers infostealers. Both loader stages use Polygon blockchain-based EtherHiding to dynamically resolve C2 infrastructure, making takedowns and blocklisting harder.

Netskope Threat Labs reports that attackers behind a previously analyzed Malware-as-a-Service NodeJS infostealer have shifted delivery methods from ClickFix-style social engineering to cloned and impersonated GitHub repositories. The repositories imitate popular AI resources and developer tools, including lures related to Claude, ComfyUI, AI coding assistants, Python security guides, and Rust frameworks. The campaign mainly targets AI users and developers in North America, Asia, and Southern Europe, with financial services, banking, and technology sectors leading among affected segments.

The malicious download arrives as a four-file zip archive containing a LuaJIT runtime DLL, a renamed LuaJIT interpreter, a batch script, and a text file containing obfuscated Lua code. The first-stage Lua script is identified as Prometheus-obfuscated, while the second-stage script shows structural indicators consistent with MoonSec V3. The payload design makes the harmful behavior appear only when all files are present and launched together, while the text file and interpreter may appear harmless when inspected separately.

The campaign uses SmartLoader twice in a redundant multi-stage chain, and both loader stages resolve their command-and-control server address from a Polygon smart contract at runtime using EtherHiding. SmartLoader collects geolocation data, captures a screenshot, sends an encrypted beacon, receives tasking, establishes persistence through a scheduled task, and downloads additional payloads from GitHub-hosted files. Netskope states that compromising developer environments is significant because developers often have access to source code, cloud credentials, API keys, code-signing certificates, and CI/CD pipelines, creating the potential for software supply chain attacks.

  • The campaign’s loader chain is intentionally redundant: SmartLoader is deployed twice, and both stages use the same Polygon smart contract to resolve infrastructure, so blocking only one stage may not stop the full infection flow.
  • The malicious Lua code is stored in a plain text file and only becomes active when executed with the bundled LuaJIT interpreter and DLL, which can evade security checks that inspect files individually rather than as a combined package.
  • The use of EtherHiding lets the attackers change the command-and-control IP address by updating a smart contract value, allowing them to redirect deployed malware without changing the payload itself.
  • The first and second loader stages use different Lua obfuscators, Prometheus and likely MoonSec V3, which increases analysis complexity across an otherwise similar attack flow.
  • The GitHub lures rely on cloned repositories that still appear authentic at the root level and may list the original contributor, making installation instructions and download URLs especially important places to verify.

In plain words

Researchers found three serious flaws in Hugging Face’s Diffusers tool that could let a specially prepared model download quietly run an attacker’s code on the computer that loads it, even when a safety setting meant to block that is off. This affects users who load Diffusers models with custom pipelines, and the problems were fixed in version 0.38.0. It matters because Hugging Face model repositories are widely used in business AI systems, build pipelines, and container images, so something that looks like a normal model download could become a way for attackers to get into those environments.

Summary
Three high-severity flaws in Hugging Face’s Diffusers library, dubbed FaceHugger, could let malicious model repositories bypass trust_remote_code protections and execute arbitrary code when loaded. Users should upgrade to Diffusers 0.38.0 or only load audited, trusted model snapshots and custom pipelines.

Three high-severity flaws have been disclosed in Hugging Face’s Diffusers library that could allow crafted model repositories to execute arbitrary code on machines that load them. Zafran Labs researchers Gal Zaban and Ido Shani said the vulnerabilities bypass trust_remote_code, a safeguard meant to stop unreviewed code from running during custom pipeline loading. The issues have been collectively named FaceHugger.

Diffusers is a Python package for pretrained diffusion models used to generate videos, images, and audio, and the article says it was downloaded more than 8.1 million times in July 2026. The article notes that Hugging Face libraries and repositories are prevalent in enterprise environments, including production pipelines, CI/CD systems, and container images. Because of that reach, the researchers warned that routine model loading can become an initial-access vector when repository artifacts are treated as passive data.

The vulnerabilities are CVE-2026-44827, CVE-2026-45804, and CVE-2026-44513, involving code injection and a race condition in the DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained loading process. Zafran said the root cause is that the trust check occurs only in the first phase, while model download behavior uses two sequential, non-atomic HTTP requests instead of a single atomic operation. The flaws were addressed in Diffusers version 0.38.0, and maintainers recommended using only trusted and audited sources, avoiding certain cross-repository custom_pipeline use, and inspecting local snapshots for unexpected Python files if patching is not immediately possible.

  • The trust_remote_code safeguard failed because the trust check occurred only in the first phase of loading, while later loading steps could still encounter custom code that had not been checked.
  • The vulnerabilities stemmed from model downloads being handled as two sequential, non-atomic HTTP requests, which created a window for repository contents or configuration to differ between check and use.
  • A model repository should not be treated as passive data, because configuration files, loaders, and custom pipeline code can turn a routine model load into code execution.
  • One workaround specifically targets hidden code placement by requiring inspection for unexpected Python files not only at the snapshot root but also inside component subdirectories such as unet and scheduler.
  • The affected Diffusers package had more than 8.1 million downloads in July 2026, showing that a flaw in this library can have broad reach across enterprise AI pipelines, CI/CD systems, and container images.
Key Points
  • 01Three high-severity flaws in Hugging Face’s Diffusers library, collectively named FaceHugger, could allow crafted model repositories to execute arbitrary code on machines that load them.
  • 02Zafran Labs researchers said the vulnerabilities bypass the trust_remote_code safeguard that is intended to stop unreviewed code from running during custom pipeline loading.
  • 03The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-44827, CVE-2026-45804, and CVE-2026-44513, and include code injection and race condition issues tied to the DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained loading process.
  • 04The vulnerabilities were addressed in Diffusers version 0.38.0, released in early May 2026, and any user who invokes DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained with custom pipelines is impacted.
  • 05Project maintainers recommended that users who cannot immediately patch only use trusted and audited sources, avoid pointing custom_pipeline to a different Hub repository before reading its pipeline.py, and inspect local snapshots for unexpected Python files.

Researchers found 18 harmful software packages on npm that were made to look like tools used by Alibaba developers, especially in Chinese-speaking work environments. Summary
Researchers found 18 malicious npm packages targeting Alibaba tool users with a cross-platform RAT, using dependency chains that impersonate private Alibaba packages to infect Chinese-speaking developer environments. Anyone who installed the packages should assume compromise, rotate credentials from a clean machine, and audit systems for suspicious activity.

Cybersecurity researchers discovered 18 malicious npm packages targeting users of Alibaba developer tools with a cross-platform remote access trojan. The campaign impersonated private Alibaba-related packages and appears aimed at Chinese-speaking developer environments. One package, lib-mtop, was first published in November 2023 without functionality, but later versions added a loader that fetched and executed a remote JavaScript payload.

The attack split malicious functionality across multiple packages in the same dependency tree, with lure packages depending on smart-config-manager as a bridge to lower-layer packages containing loader logic. A rule engine used the vm module to choose payload behavior based on the victim’s operating system, and the payload was retrieved from a domain made to resemble Alibaba infrastructure. On Windows it targeted Alilang, on Linux it downloaded and ran a binary from /tmp, and on macOS it modified ~/.zshrc and created a Launch Agent.

The final payload is described as a complex backdoor with command execution, file upload and download, host reconnaissance, payload staging, and lateral movement capabilities. It can also persist by injecting malicious code into enterprise collaboration applications such as DingTalk, Wukong, and Qoder. Users who installed any listed package are advised to assume compromise, rotate sensitive credentials from a clean machine, and audit developer systems for suspicious activity.

  • The attack hid its malicious loader across several otherwise separate npm packages, meaning a single package may appear harmless unless the full dependency tree is examined together.
  • The lure packages were designed to work normally in environments that had access to the real private Alibaba packages, while also installing extra malicious dependencies.
  • The payload download domain was made to resemble Alibaba infrastructure, which could help the activity blend into normal developer network traffic.
  • The final backdoor included lateral-spread capabilities and persistence through enterprise collaboration applications, so the risk extends beyond the initial developer machine.
  • The campaign’s low download counts do not necessarily indicate low impact because the packages appear to have been aimed at a narrow set of Alibaba-related developer environments.

  • 01Cybersecurity researchers discovered 18 malicious npm packages targeting users of Alibaba developer tools with a cross-platform remote access trojan in a targeted software supply chain campaign against Chinese-speaking environments.
  • 02The package lib-mtop was published under the same unscoped name as a private Alibaba package, and later versions added a loader that fetches and executes a remote JavaScript payload using curl.
  • 03The campaign split malicious loader functionality across multiple packages in the same dependency tree, with top-layer packages impersonating private @ali-scoped packages and smart-config-manager acting as a middle-layer bridge.
  • 04The payload behaves differently by operating system, including trojanizing Alilang on Windows, downloading and running a temporary binary on Linux, and adding a background script and Launch Agent on macOS.
  • 05Users who installed any of the listed packages are advised to assume compromise, rotate sensitive credentials from a clean machine, and audit developer systems for suspicious activity.

A new Russian service called DOUBLECUP helps criminals build fake website prompts, such as fake CAPTCHA pages, that trick people into pasting and running a command copied to their clipboard. That command pulls hidden malicious code out of images saved in the person’s browser cache and can install harmful programs on Windows and macOS devices. People visiting fake login pages pretending to be services like NetSuite, Odoo, HubSpot, and Salesforce could be affected. This matters because the installed programs can collect information about the device, stay on it, download more files, and let attackers send commands while making their control servers harder to shut down.

Summary
A new Russian loader-as-a-service called DOUBLECUP is using ClickFix lures to make victims run commands that extract malware hidden in cached PNG images. The campaigns deliver CountLoader on Windows and macOS and a new Windows RAT called DeviceManager, which uses smart contracts and DNS records for resilient command-and-control.

A new Russian loader-as-a-service named DOUBLECUP uses ClickFix attacks to hide malicious code in PNG images cached by victims’ browsers. SOCRadar says the service has operated since early June 2026 and provides customers with licenses and a Go-based Windows tool for creating malicious campaigns. The attacks ultimately deliver CountLoader to Windows and macOS devices and a new remote access trojan named DeviceManager to Windows systems.

DOUBLECUP handles infrastructure such as hosting steganographic PNG images, managing session and signal endpoints, providing encryption keys, and automatically rebuilding payloads. Customers create and host the websites that display fake ClickFix prompts, add generated frontend code, and implement any extra obfuscation or anti-analysis measures. SOCRadar observed fake CAPTCHA prompts on login pages impersonating NetSuite, Odoo, HubSpot, and Salesforce, with malicious code loaded through embedded iframes.

When a victim visits one of these sites, DOUBLECUP registers the session, determines the victim’s public IP address, and forces the browser to download and cache a malicious PNG image. If the victim runs the copied command, it searches the browser cache for the PNG by exact file size and uses findstr or certutil to recover and execute the hidden first-stage payload. The final payloads include CountLoader, which harvests system information and can download and execute files, and DeviceManager, a Python-based Windows RAT that uses blockchain smart contracts and DNS records for command-and-control activity.

  • DOUBLECUP reduces the operational burden for its customers by hosting steganographic PNG images, managing session and signal endpoints, providing encryption keys, and automatically rebuilding payloads, while customers only need to host the lure sites and add the generated code.
  • The malicious command is customized for the victim’s specific browser, with DOUBLECUP generating commands for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, and Opera.
  • The attack ties payload decryption to the victim’s public IPv4 address, which the second-stage dropper uses to create the decryption key for the final encrypted payload.
  • DeviceManager avoids using a fixed command-and-control address by retrieving its current server IP from Ethereum or Polygon smart contracts through a technique called EtherHiding.
  • DeviceManager uses DNS A and TXT records not only to steal system information but also to retrieve commands, download payloads, and return command output to attackers.

  • 04When victims run the copied command, it searches the browser cache for the malicious PNG by exact file size and uses findstr or certutil to recover and execute the hidden first-stage payload.

    Criminals are sharing fake versions of a Roblox tool called Xeno Executor through gaming forums, Discord communities, and impersonated accounts, tricking players into installing harmful software instead. Roblox players who run these fake installers can have browser data, gaming accounts, payment details, cryptocurrency wallet information, screenshots, webcam access, and control of their computer stolen. This matters because a cheat or script tool advertised as “undetected” can become a way for attackers to spy on people and take over their accounts and devices.

    Summary
    Fake Xeno Executor installers targeting Roblox players are spreading a Java-based RAT and infostealer that steals browser data, gaming and payment account tokens, crypto wallets, and enables surveillance and remote control. Players should avoid third-party Roblox tools from unofficial sources, especially “undetected” versions shared on forums or Discord.

    Fake Xeno Executor installers are infecting Roblox players with malware that provides remote access and steals sensitive information. Xeno Executor is a popular Roblox utility used to run scripts, including cheats, and attackers are promoting fake versions as “undetected” releases. Bitdefender found the campaign has targeted Roblox users since the start of the year, rising sharply in March before stabilizing.

    The fake installers are promoted through gaming forums, Discord communities, and compromised or impersonated accounts controlled by the attackers. Victims download ZIP archives or self-extracting archives that include instructions and are made to look authentic by recreating a legitimate Xeno installation structure, including genuine Lua scripts and plausible filenames. When victims run xeno.exe, they actually launch the first-stage malware loader.

    The malware checks for a Java Runtime Environment, extracts one if needed, and launches an obfuscated Java payload disguised as decompiler.exe that registers the victim and downloads the final payload. The final Java-based tool can steal browser data, online account and payment information, Discord, Roblox, Minecraft, and Microsoft Store tokens, and cryptocurrency wallet data including Exodus Wallet data. It also supports keylogging, mouse activity logging, screenshots, desktop streaming, webcam access, file transfers, PowerShell command execution, and interactive remote shell access.

    • The attackers exploit the normal cycle of Roblox blocking existing Xeno Executor versions by advertising their fake installer as a new “undetected” release, making the lure more believable to users seeking to bypass anti-cheat protections.

    • The malware’s use of Java includes checking for a Java Runtime Environment and extracting one if needed, which helps the attack proceed even on systems where Java is not already installed.
    • Bitdefender believes this campaign is related to the previously documented “Powercat” activity but has significant capability updates and new command-and-control infrastructure, showing that the operation is continuing to evolve.

In plain words

Attackers are sharing fake versions of the Xeno Roblox cheat tool through gaming forums and Discord, tricking players into running harmful software instead of the cheat they expected. People looking for Roblox cheats, including children and teenagers, can have their Discord, Roblox, Minecraft, browser, crypto wallet, and payment information stolen from the infected computer. The software can also watch what the person types, capture the screen or webcam, change files, and let the attackers control the computer, which could expose private conversations, family financial information, and online accounts.

Summary
Attackers are spreading fake “undetected” Xeno Roblox cheat packages through Discord and gaming forums to infect players with a multi-stage Java stealer known as Powercat. The malware can steal gaming, Discord, browser, crypto wallet and payment data, while also enabling webcam access, keylogging, desktop streaming, PowerShell execution and remote control of the victim’s PC.

Bitdefender researchers describe a malware campaign disguised as an “undetected” version of the Xeno Roblox script executor. The fake cheat is promoted through gaming forums and Discord communities and targets players looking to download what appears to be a legitimate Roblox tool. The campaign has affected users since the beginning of the year, with activity rising sharply in the second half of March.

The infection uses a multi-stage Java chain designed to look legitimate by imitating Xeno files, using Windows-style names, and hiding inside trusted-looking directories such as a folder associated with Microsoft GameDVR. The first stage runs a fake xeno.exe, installs or uses a Java runtime, and launches a JAR disguised as decompiler.exe. Later stages perform environment checks, communicate with command-and-control servers, and place a Java stealer in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR using DLL-like filenames.

The final payload can steal browser cookies, Discord, Roblox and Minecraft accounts, cryptocurrency wallet data, and payment-related tokens. It can also record keystrokes, access the webcam, capture screenshots, stream the victim’s desktop, manipulate files, run PowerShell commands, and provide interactive control of the infected computer. Bitdefender says newly identified command-and-control infrastructure and expanded functionality suggest the malware, previously documented by ThreatLocker as Powercat, remains under active development.

  • The fake Xeno package is made more convincing by including some real LUA scripts from a Xeno installation, while other files such as RbxAnalytics.png contain only small junk data.
  • The first-stage loader installs its own Java Runtime Environment under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe if Java is missing, allowing the infection chain to run even on systems without Java already installed.
  • The third-stage payload hides in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR using DLL-like names and persists through a Run key named “Display Calibration,” blending with Windows and gaming-related components.
  • The malware does not only copy Exodus wallet files; it checks for Exodus version 26.1.5, modifies the local application by injecting JavaScript, and collects wallet-related data written during runtime.
  • Bitdefender observed infections since the beginning of the year, with activity rising sharply in the second half of March and then maintaining a relatively consistent infection rate.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers are distributing malware disguised as an “undetected” version of the Xeno Roblox script executor through gaming forums and Discord communities.
  • 02The campaign uses a multi-stage Java infection chain in which files and folders imitate legitimate Xeno, Windows, and gaming components, including use of a Microsoft GameDVR-related directory.
  • 03The final payload can steal browser cookies, Discord, Roblox and Minecraft accounts, cryptocurrency wallet data, and payment-related information.
  • 04The malware can also record keystrokes, access the webcam, stream the victim’s desktop, manipulate files, run PowerShell commands, and provide attackers with interactive control of the infected computer.
  • 05Bitdefender researchers identified new command-and-control infrastructure and additional capabilities, suggesting the malware previously documented as Powercat remains under active development.

    Researchers found that harmful software already running on a Windows computer can misuse Google Password Manager in Chrome to sign in to some accounts protected by passkeys, without showing anything on the screen or asking for a fingerprint or PIN. This affects people using Chrome’s Google Password Manager on Windows computers with a TPM, and it depends on the device already being infected. It matters because passkeys themselves are not broken, but a stolen or infected computer may still let an attacker get into accounts or keep access later if websites and password managers do not check carefully enough.

    Summary
    Unit 42 found that malware already running on a Windows device could abuse Chrome’s Google Password Manager passkey handling to silently authenticate, enroll attacker-controlled verification keys, or extract synced passkey secrets. The issue does not break passkey cryptography, but shows that compromised endpoints and weak relying-party UV checks can still lead to passkey-protected account takeover.

    Unit 42 detailed three attack paths against Chrome’s Google Password Manager cloud authenticator on Windows systems with a Trusted Platform Module. The techniques, named Pass-ta-key, Silver Pass-ta-key, and Golden Pass-ta-key, all begin with malware already running on the victim’s device. The article says the attacks do not break passkey cryptography, but target the code and processes around how Chrome stores device keys, re-enrolls devices, and handles user-verification checks.

    The attacks can silently obtain a valid authentication assertion, install an attacker-controlled user-verification key, or extract the 32-byte Security Domain Secret used to decrypt synced passkey private keys. The researchers said the last two paths can provide reusable access from an attacker’s own environment after the initial endpoint compromise. The report does not describe exploitation in the wild and gives no CVE identifiers, affected Chrome versions, or complete remediation status.

    The article says relying parties should set userVerification to required and verify the returned User Verified bit, noting that GitHub enforced the check while eBay accepted a test assertion until fixing the validation gap after disclosure. It also says credential providers should attest newly enrolled keys, strengthen re-registration and recovery checks, restrict access to local passkey state, and keep master keys out of client logs and memory. The reviewed sources do not say whether changing the Google Password Manager PIN or deleting Password Manager data invalidates a secret an attacker already holds.

    • The most immediately actionable defense for websites is to set userVerification to required and verify that the returned User Verified bit is present, because the article says GitHub blocked this path while eBay initially accepted the test assertion until fixing its validation gap.
    • The attacks show that passkey security can depend heavily on implementation details outside the cryptography, such as Chrome’s storage of device keys, device re-enrollment behavior, and whether websites enforce user-verification checks.
    • The strongest attack path targets the 32-byte Security Domain Secret, but the article says public documentation does not describe an SDS-specific rotation or revocation option for users who suspect exposure.
    • The article notes there were no matching CVEs in the National Vulnerability Database and no public Google or eBay notices documenting the reported changes as of August 3, 2026, leaving the remediation status unclear.
    • Chromium source corroborates architectural details such as TPM key handling and plaintext SDS presence in Chrome memory, but the article distinguishes that from proof that the latest stable Chrome release remains exploitable.
    Key Points
    • 01Unit 42 detailed three attack paths against Chrome's Google Password Manager cloud authenticator, named Pass-ta-key, Silver Pass-ta-key, and Golden Pass-ta-key.
    • 02The attacks require malware already running as an ordinary user on a victim's Windows device with a Trusted Platform Module and do not break passkey cryptography.
    • 03Pass-ta-key can obtain a valid authentication assertion with the User Verified flag unset, which should be rejected by relying parties that require user verification under the Web Authentication specification.

In plain words

Researchers found three ways that harmful software already running on a Windows computer can misuse Google Password Manager’s saved passkeys in Chrome to help break into a person’s online accounts. People using Google-synced passkeys on an already-compromised Windows device are the ones affected, and some websites can be at higher risk if they do not properly check that the real user confirmed the sign-in. This matters because passkeys are safer than passwords in many ways, but they do not fully protect accounts when the computer itself has been taken over.

Summary
Researchers found three “Pass-ta-key” attacks that let malware already running on a Windows device abuse Google Password Manager’s synced passkeys to bypass verification or extract private keys. The findings show passkeys are still vulnerable when the user’s device is compromised, especially if services fail to properly validate user verification.

Security researchers at Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 discovered three attacks, collectively called Pass-ta-key, that target Google Password Manager in Chrome on already-compromised Windows devices with a Trusted Platform Module. The attacks can abuse Google-synced passkeys to take over accounts, bypass user verification, or extract passkey private keys. The researchers said the attacks do not break passkey cryptography, but instead exploit weaknesses in how Chrome and Google’s cloud authenticator handle device trust, onboarding, recovery, and synced credentials.

The first Pass-ta-key technique lets unprivileged malware impersonate a trusted device and request a valid authentication response from Google’s cloud authenticator without administrator privileges, user interaction, biometrics, or unlocking the device. This can fail when a service properly checks the User Verified flag, as GitHub did, but Unit 42 said it succeeded against eBay because eBay did not properly validate that flag despite requiring user verification. eBay fixed the issue after the researchers reported it.

The Silver Pass-ta-key technique allows attackers to register their own user-verification key with Google’s cloud authenticator, while the Golden Pass-ta-key technique allows malware to obtain the security domain secret used to encrypt synced passkeys. Unit 42 said Google removed the secret from Chrome’s FIDO logs after disclosure, but the secret is still sent to Chrome and remains temporarily accessible in browser process memory. The researchers warned that the stolen master key could decrypt current and future synced passkeys, and recommended that websites properly validate user verification and that credential managers harden device registration, recovery, and master key handling.

  • A service can require user verification and still be vulnerable if it does not properly validate the User Verified flag, as Unit 42 demonstrated with eBay before the issue was fixed.
  • The first Pass-ta-key attack does not require administrator privileges, user interaction, biometrics, or unlocking the device, which makes local malware more dangerous than many users may assume.
  • Google removed the security domain secret from Chrome's FIDO logs after disclosure, but Unit 42 said the secret is still sent to Chrome and remains temporarily accessible in browser process memory.
  • Unit 42 said Google's current implementation provides no way to rotate or revoke the stolen security domain secret, meaning current and future synced passkeys remain protected by the same secret.
  • The researchers' recommendations place responsibility not only on Google Password Manager but also on websites, which need to require and properly validate user verification for passkey logins.
Key Points
  • 01Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 discovered three attacks, collectively called "Pass-ta-key," that target Google Password Manager in Chrome on already-compromised Windows devices with a Trusted Platform Module.
  • 02The first Pass-ta-key technique lets unprivileged malware impersonate a trusted device and request a valid passkey authentication response from Google's cloud authenticator without administrator privileges, user interaction, biometrics, or unlocking the device.
  • 03The Silver Pass-ta-key technique allows attackers to register their own user-verification key with Google's cloud authenticator, enabling access to accounts that properly require and validate user verification.
  • 04The Golden Pass-ta-key technique allows malware to obtain the security domain secret used to encrypt synced passkeys, which can then be used to decrypt passkey records and recover private keys.
  • 05Unit 42 said passkeys remain significantly safer than traditional passwords, but the attacks show they do not eliminate the risks posed by malware already running on a compromised device.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific, novel research finding affecting Google Password Manager synced passkeys in Chrome on Windows, with demonstrated account-takeover implications and concrete affected services such as eBay. It is broadly relevant for security professionals because it challenges assumptions about passkey protections, but it is not described as active exploitation in the wild and requires malware already running on the victim device.

In plain words

Hackers broke into Liechtenstein’s register that lists the real people behind companies, foundations, and trusts, and stole records connected to 31,000 entities. This affects people and organizations tied to those legal entities, in a country that is a major wealth management hub for clients around the world. The government took the affected systems offline and formed a crisis team, and officials say they have not found evidence that the information was changed or deleted. The incident matters because government records like these can contain sensitive information that criminals or spies may try to use.

Summary
Hackers accessed Liechtenstein’s Register of Beneficial Owners for two days and stole data on about 31,000 companies, foundations and trusts. The government took affected systems offline and formed a crisis unit, with no evidence so far that records were altered or deleted.

A cyberattack compromised tens of thousands of records related to companies, foundations and trusts in Liechtenstein. Unknown attackers gained access to the country’s Register of Beneficial Owners for two days beginning on July 29. The register contains information on who owns legal entities in the country and was created in 2021 in accordance with European Union rules around money laundering and financial transparency.

The Office of Justice, which houses the registry, first noticed the intrusion, and the affected systems were quickly taken offline. An initial investigation found that data related to 31,000 entities was exfiltrated. The government said there is no evidence that information was modified or deleted.

Liechtenstein’s government formed a crisis team headed by Prime Minister Brigitte Haas and Minister of Justice Emanuel Schädler to address the breach. The incident is significant because Liechtenstein is a financial services powerhouse and wealth management hub for clients around the world despite having about 40,000 residents. The article notes that cyberattacks targeting government registries are common and can give cybercriminals and spies access to large amounts of sensitive data.

  • The scale of the stolen data is striking because Liechtenstein has about 40,000 residents, yet the breach involved records tied to 31,000 legal entities.
  • The compromised register exists to support financial transparency and anti-money-laundering rules, showing that systems created for accountability can also become high-value targets because they identify the people behind legal entities.
  • The government’s response was elevated to the national leadership level, with a crisis team headed by the prime minister and justice minister.
  • The article places the incident in a broader pattern of government registry compromises, citing multiple recent incidents in France involving identity documents, education records and bank-account records.
Key Points
  • 01Unknown attackers accessed Liechtenstein’s Register of Beneficial Owners for two days beginning on July 29.
  • 02An initial investigation found that data related to 31,000 entities was exfiltrated, with no evidence that information was modified or deleted.
  • 03The Office of Justice, which houses the registry, noticed the intrusion and the affected systems were quickly taken offline.
  • 04Liechtenstein’s government formed a crisis team headed by Prime Minister Brigitte Haas and Minister of Justice Emanuel Schädler to address the breach.
  • 05The register contains information on who owns legal entities in Liechtenstein and was created in 2021 under European Union rules on money laundering and financial transparency.

In plain words

A mid-size business received an email with a PDF that looked like a normal statement, but the whole page was secretly clickable and opened a fake Adobe Acrobat page meant to steal login details. The email looked trustworthy because the sender’s domain passed normal checks, and the words in the message were hidden from filters in ways that still looked normal to a person. This matters because an employee could trigger the trap just by clicking anywhere on the document, and attacks like this show how ordinary work attachments can be turned into credential theft.

Summary
A malicious statement-themed PDF hid a full-page invisible button that launched JavaScript to open an Adobe-branded credential phishing page, despite appearing inert and passing email authentication. The key lesson is that PDF analysis must inspect annotation geometry and click-triggered actions, not just auto-run scripts or visible links.

A statement-themed PDF reached a shared ordering mailbox at a mid-size business from an aged sender domain that passed SPF and DMARC. The attachment rendered as a flat image with no visible controls, no auto-run action, and no interactive form registration. The platform verdict was malicious, and IRONSCALES reported that its Adaptive AI analyst, Themis, resolved the message as phishing autonomously with mitigation recorded roughly two seconds after receipt.

The PDF contained a pushbutton widget annotation sized to the full page, with a rectangle matching the media box dimensions. That annotation pointed to embedded JavaScript calling app.launchURL to open hxxps://acrobat-v215219-plug[.]web[.]app, a Firebase-hosted page using the Acrobat name for an Adobe-branded credential harvesting lure. The article emphasizes that the redirect did not auto-fire, but any click anywhere on the page could trigger the action.

The email body used invisible soft hyphens to break words such as “please,” “attached,” “order,” and “statement,” while the signature split a secondary contact address with empty HTML comment markers. The sender domain chengtouzs[.]com had its own SPF record authorizing the sending host, DMARC passed under a quarantine policy, and the domain later lapsed into redemption. The article maps the activity to MITRE ATT&CK techniques for spearphishing attachment, malicious link user execution, and obfuscated files or information.

  • A PDF can avoid auto-run indicators yet still behave almost like an automatic redirect if an invisible click target covers the entire page.
  • Checking only whether a PDF contains JavaScript is less useful than identifying what object can trigger it and how large that trigger area is.
  • A missing AcroForm dictionary can be suspicious when a button widget is present, because the article describes this as a sign of an overlay added to an existing page rather than a normal form.
  • Email authentication passing did not make the message trustworthy, because the sender controlled the domain and published SPF records that authorized the sending host.
  • Text filters can miss words that humans read normally if the message uses invisible soft hyphens or HTML comment markers, so analysis should normalize text before matching on it.
Key Points
  • 01A one-page statement-themed PDF sent to a shared ordering mailbox contained a pushbutton widget annotation whose rectangle matched the full page dimensions.
  • 02The PDF annotation was wired to embedded JavaScript that called app.launchURL to open hxxps://acrobat-v215219-plug[.]web[.]app, a Firebase-hosted page borrowing the Acrobat name.
  • 03The PDF did not contain a document OpenAction, a document-level JavaScript name tree, or an AcroForm dictionary, making it appear inert in several structural checks.
  • 04The email body broke visible words apart with invisible soft hyphens, and the signature split a secondary contact address with empty HTML comment markers.
  • 05The sender domain chengtouzs[.]com passed SPF and DMARC because its own SPF record authorized the sending host, and the domain later lapsed into a redemption period.

In plain words

The article looks at attacks on schools and universities in Brazil that Kaspersky investigated from January 2025 to June 2026, including cases where criminals locked files for ransom and one case where someone inside an institution secretly recorded passwords. Students, parents, teachers, staff, and the institutions themselves can be affected because school systems often hold personal details like ID numbers, addresses, phone numbers, and parents’ names. If this information is stolen or accounts are misused, criminals can impersonate people, trick them with fake messages, or disrupt classes and administrative work.

Summary
Kaspersky’s incident response cases show Brazilian educational institutions are being hit by ransomware and insider threats largely through common weaknesses like stolen valid accounts, exposed services, remote access tools, shared accounts, and poor patching. The key defenses are MFA, least privilege, elimination of shared accounts, hardened endpoints, tested isolated backups, and stronger forensic logging.

Kaspersky’s Global Emergency Response Team analyzed incident response cases affecting Brazilian educational institutions from January 2025 to June 2026. The cases involved public and private schools and universities, with most incidents in São Paulo and additional cases in Rio de Janeiro and Pernambuco. The article says these institutions are frequent targets because they hold large amounts of personal data and operate complex environments used by students, professors, researchers, staff, contractors, and visitors.

High-severity incidents made up 40% of the cases and were mainly ransomware attacks, while the remaining 60% were medium severity. Private institutions were most often affected by ransomware, including DragonForce and LockBit 3, while public institutions more often saw suspicious endpoint activity and privilege escalation attempts. The most common initial access vectors were valid accounts, exploitation of public-facing applications, and insiders, and attackers used tools such as AnyDesk, PsExec, AV-killer malware, and Potato privilege-escalation variants.

The article describes cases involving a custom LockBit variant built from a leaked builder, DragonForce deployed after AnyDesk installation through a compromised account, and a Python keylogger used by an insider on a shared machine. Investigators reconstructed activity using forensic artifacts such as Prefetch, Amcache.hve, PCA, UserAssist, MFT, and the USN Journal, even where logs were erased. The recommendations include enforcing multi-factor authentication, reviewing privileged accounts, eliminating shared accounts, monitoring remote access tools, isolating and testing backups, centralizing logs, and improving patch management.

  • Private educational institutions in the dataset were more often targeted by ransomware, while public institutions’ incidents were mostly tied to suspicious endpoint activity and privilege escalation attempts.
  • Several incidents relied on ordinary weaknesses rather than advanced techniques, including valid accounts, exposed applications, inadequate patch management, and publicly available tools known to attackers.
  • Even when attackers erased system logs, investigators recovered useful evidence from artifacts such as Prefetch, Amcache.hve, PCA, UserAssist, MFT, and the USN Journal.
  • Some institutions were still using Windows 10 after its October 2025 end-of-support date and unpatched Windows Server 2016 systems, which increased both exposure to known vulnerabilities and the difficulty of forensic collection.
  • The insider keylogger case showed that shared user accounts on multi-user machines can prevent clear attribution even when investigators identify the malicious files, execution evidence, and likely USB-based log retrieval.
Key Points
  • 01Kaspersky’s Global Emergency Response Team analyzed incident response cases involving Brazilian educational institutions from January 2025 to June 2026, with most cases occurring in São Paulo and additional cases in Rio de Janeiro and Pernambuco.
  • 02High-severity incidents accounted for 40% of the cases and were mainly ransomware attacks, with DragonForce and LockBit 3 among the most common ransomware families observed.
  • 03The most common initial access vectors were valid accounts, exploitation of public-facing applications, and insiders, while privilege escalation often involved Potato variants such as GodPotato, SweetPotato, and BadPotato.
  • 04The investigations found attackers using AnyDesk for remote access, PsExec for lateral movement, and AV-killer malware to disable defenses, especially in ransomware-related incidents.
  • 05The article recommends multi-factor authentication for public services, reviews of privileged accounts, elimination of shared accounts, monitoring of remote access tools, isolated and tested backups, centralized logging, and effective patch management.
